questions.question: What is the core economic benefit of 'separation of compute and storage' in a cloud warehouse like Snowflake or BigQuery?
options: It makes queries run instantaneously regardless of data volume
Storage and compute can scale and be billed independently, so you only pay for compute when a query actually runs
It removes the need for any data governance
It guarantees zero egress fees
questions.explanation: On-premise systems bundle storage and compute into one fixed-cost server. Cloud warehouses decouple them: storage is cheap and persistent, while compute (the 'staff') is spun up only when a query runs and billed per-second/credit. This elasticity is why a Tuesday with 5 users and a New Year's Eve spike with 500 users can both be cost-efficient.

questions.question: BrightCart's events table holds 18 months of history at 40M rows/day. A dashboard query filters WHERE event_date >= CURRENT_DATE - 90 and the table is clustered on event_date. What happens to bytes scanned?
options: All 18 months are scanned regardless of the filter
Only the last 90 days of partitions are scanned — roughly an 83% reduction in this lesson's worked example
BigQuery/Snowflake ignore filters on date columns
Scanned bytes increase because filtering adds overhead
questions.explanation: This is partition pruning: the query engine uses partition/micro-partition metadata to skip files that cannot contain matching rows. In the Day 83 costed-design exercise, pruning to a 90-day window out of 540 days of history cuts scanned bytes from ~3.89 TB to ~648 GB per query — about an 83% reduction, and a fixed, bounded cost even as history keeps growing.

questions.question: Why is `SELECT * FROM logs` dangerous in a pay-per-bytes-scanned warehouse like BigQuery?
options: It will fail to execute
Even if the result set is small, you are billed for every byte the query scans, so a 1 PB logs table can cost thousands of dollars in seconds
SELECT * is only dangerous in row-store databases
It only matters if the query returns rows
questions.explanation: Byte-scan pricing charges for data read, not data returned. A 1 PB logs table scanned by SELECT * can produce a five-figure bill in seconds — the lesson's '$10,000 query' danger. Defenses include quotas/limits, forcing partition filters, and monitoring top spenders daily.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the IAM/networking/compliance baseline this lesson requires before calling a Modern Data Stack 'production-ready'?
options: Least-privilege roles so an analyst role cannot query the payroll schema
Private connectivity (PrivateLink/Private Service Connect) instead of exposing the warehouse to the public internet
Hardcoding the warehouse password directly in profiles.yml and committing it to Git for convenience
Confirming SOC 2/ISO 27001/HIPAA certifications match your industry's requirements before committing to a vendor
questions.explanation: Secrets (passwords, API tokens, Reverse ETL credentials) belong in a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault), never hardcoded into a committed config file. The other three options are all real parts of the security baseline: least-privilege IAM, private networking, and compliance verification.

questions.question: A FinOps program wants to bill the Marketing team's BI spend back to their cost center for accountability, without enforcing a hard cap. Which FinOps control is this?
options: A budget
A quota
Chargeback (or, without an actual bill, showback)
Autoscaling
questions.explanation: Chargeback bills the cost back to the requesting team's budget; showback simply reports it without an actual transfer of funds. Budgets are spending caps, quotas limit resource consumption (e.g., bytes scanned/day), and autoscaling is a compute-elasticity mechanism, not a cost-attribution one.

questions.question: According to the Day 83 decision guide, why might a 3-person startup with 50K rows in Postgres be wrong to adopt Snowflake + Fivetran + dbt immediately?
options: Snowflake cannot handle small datasets

The Modern Data Stack adds licensing, operational, and learning overhead that isn't justified until you have multiple source systems, governed self-serve needs, or analytical query loads an OLTP database struggles with
dbt only works with BigQuery
Fivetran requires a minimum of 10 employees to use
questions.explanation: The lesson's 'when not to use MDS' callout argues that a well-indexed Postgres replica with a BI tool pointed at it is faster to ship and far cheaper for small, single-source, low-volume use cases. The MDS earns its complexity when there are multiple source systems, a team needing governed self-serve access, or volumes that strain a single OLTP database.

questions.question: What is the most likely hidden cost when migrating away from a cloud data warehouse vendor, according to the Pitfalls section?
options: Storage costs while data sits idle
Egress fees for moving data out, plus the multi-quarter cost of re-validating every report and retraining every analyst
There are no exit costs once you've paid for onboarding
Compute costs always drop to zero during migration
questions.explanation: Cloud vendors typically make it cheap to load data in but charge egress fees to move data out, and a full re-platform requires re-validating reports and retraining analysts over months, not a weekend. The lesson's advice is to model exit cost before committing, not after signing a contract.

questions.question: In the costed-design lab, BrightCart budgets a Small Snowflake-style warehouse running ~6 hours/day, 22 business days/month, at $2/credit-hour-equivalent ($2/hour for a Small warehouse). What is the approximate monthly compute cost?
options: $48/month
$132/month
$264/month
$528/month
questions.explanation: 6 hours/day x 22 days/month x $2/hour = $264/month. Combined with roughly $32/month of storage for 18 months of compressed clickstream data, the total lands near $296/month — comfortably inside BrightCart's $600/month cap, leaving headroom for occasional Medium-warehouse analyst bursts.
